**Proposition.** Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a category with objects representing physical systems and morphisms representing symmetry transformations. Then for any object $S$ with symmetry group $G$ acting on it, there exists a functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}'$ where $\mathcal{C}'$ has objects representing phases, such that: (1) Each symmetry-breaking morphism $\varphi: S \to S'$ in $\mathcal{C}$ maps to a distinct phase object in $\mathcal{C}'$, and (2) The kernel of the group homomorphism $\rho: G \to \text{Aut}(S')$ corresponds bijectively to emergent collective degrees of freedom in the quotient space $S/\text{Ker}(\rho)$.

**Proof.** We assume that physical systems can be represented as objects in a category $\mathcal{C}$ enriched over $\textbf{Set}$, with symmetry transformations forming functorial group actions. Let phases correspond to equivalence classes of states under residual symmetries, and suppose collective degrees of freedom can be identified with elements of appropriate quotient spaces. We further assume that symmetry breaking can be represented as a morphism reducing the automorphism group, and that there exists a well-defined notion of emergent degrees of freedom in our categorical framework.

Let $S$ be an object in $\mathcal{C}$ equipped with a $G$-action. By the definition of group actions, this induces a group homomorphism $G \to \text{Aut}(S)$, so the automorphism group $\text{Aut}(S)$ contains $G$ as a subgroup. 

Consider a symmetry-breaking morphism $\varphi: S \to S'$. By functoriality of group actions under morphisms, this induces a group homomorphism $\rho: G \to \text{Aut}(S')$. The kernel $\text{Ker}(\rho)$ consists precisely of those elements of $G$ that act trivially on $S'$, representing the symmetries that have been broken by the morphism $\varphi$.

[Note: To establish that distinct kernels correspond to distinct phases requires a precise categorical definition of 'phase' that may not exist in standard mathematical literature. We proceed under the assumption that such a correspondence can be established.]

The quotient space $S/\text{Ker}(\rho)$ represents the system modulo the broken symmetries. [Note: The existence of such quotients in general categories is not guaranteed and depends on additional structure in $\mathcal{C}$.] Elements of this quotient space that are not in the image of the canonical quotient map can be interpreted as new degrees of freedom arising from the symmetry breaking. [Note: The notion of 'emergent' degrees of freedom requires a rigorous categorical definition that we assume but do not provide here.]

We now construct the functor $F: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C}'$. For each symmetry-breaking morphism $\varphi: S \to S'$, we assign a phase object in $\mathcal{C}'$ determined by the kernel $\text{Ker}(\rho)$. [Note: The functoriality of this construction depends on showing that the assignment respects composition, which requires the unestablished correspondence between kernels and phases.]

By the First Isomorphism Theorem, we have $G/\text{Ker}(\rho) \cong \text{Im}(\rho)$. This isomorphism, combined with our construction, yields a bijection between elements of $\text{Ker}(\rho)$ and the emergent collective degrees of freedom in $S/\text{Ker}(\rho)$. [Note: This requires showing that the relevant structures form groups or modules in a compatible way, which depends on additional assumptions about the categorical framework.]

The construction draws upon fundamental results from physics: Goldstone's Theorem, which relates spontaneous breaking of continuous symmetries to massless excitations, and Landau's theory of phase transitions, which classifies phases by symmetry breaking and order parameters. These provide physical motivation for our categorical formulation.

This completes the proof, subject to the noted gaps in the categorical foundations. □
